dossier.summary: The project gives substantial analytical and simulation evidence that design leverage controls sampling error while exposure misspecification can produce persistent bias in regression-based global-effect estimates. Six-world sweeps across several synthetic graph families and two public graph topologies support the main clustering, spillover and interval-coverage trends, with explicit limitations for synthetic outcomes and approximate cluster formulas. Claims about where richer regressions reduce bias and which regression has the lowest error need qualification against the paper's own tables. Failed regular-graph settings, an inconsistent percentage denominator, mixed-setting table averages and an outdated calibration affect reported coverage or numerical comparisons. The delivered results have recorded execution provenance, but the reproduction launcher requires path and archive-handling repairs.

claims.quote: Sampling error is predictable from graph and design alone.} $\mathrm{RMSE}\approx\hat\kappa\sqrt{L/n}$ with leverage $L=(1+d_H)/(p(1-p))$ under unit randomization ($d_H$: harmonic-mean degree): error grows like $\sqrt{\text{degree}}$, shrinks like $n^{-1/2}$, and one fitted constant predicts 162 Bernoulli-design runs with median ratio $1.01$ ($98\%$ within $\pm10\%$). Cluster randomization lowers $L$ by an amount that depends on how well the graph clusters (RMSE $2.9\times$ lower on ego-Facebook, $1.9\times$ on Stanford3); the closed form is a rough guide there.

In simulations on synthetic graphs and two Facebook graphs (Stanford3, ego-Facebook) with exactly known GATE, one fitted constant predicts the RMSE of 162 Bernoulli-design runs (median ratio $1.01$, $98\%$ within $10\%$) and the bias formulas match simulation to within about $0.01$--$0.02$ on a GATE of $2$.
scope_words: synthetic graphs and two Facebook graphs

claims.quote: Design matters as much as the estimator.} Clustering cuts leverage and, where the graph clusters well, bias (multi-hop bias $-0.71\to-0.11$ on ego-Facebook, $-0.85\to-0.49$ on Stanford3, little on ER/SBM); the treated fraction and number of clusters trade bias for variance.
richer regressions reduce bias only where the graph supplies extreme exposures (a cubic fixes Stanford3/ego-Facebook for $15$--$45\%$ extra RMSE but has RMSE $\approx2$ on near-regular graphs)
Regression beats DiM only if spillover exceeds $\approx\hat\kappa\sqrt{L/n}$ ($\ge0.8\beta$ for $n{=}10^3$, $d{=}128$)
sandwich intervals cover well when the model is right (mean $0.95$) and fail when it is not (mean $0.57$), the failure being explained by the bias.

In our experiments the RMSE of the regression GATE estimator is well described by $\sqrt{B^2+\hat\kappa^2L/n}$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:ext}d). $L$ depends only on graph and design and can be computed \emph{before} an experiment (Prop.~\ref{prop:lev}): it grows with the harmonic-mean degree and $1/(p(1-p))$ and is cut by clusterings that keep neighbourhoods together. $B$ is what the regression cannot represent: the response slope away from the exposures the design visits, interference beyond the modelled neighbourhood, and effect heterogeneity correlated with a unit's exposure variance. More data does not cure a nonzero $B$; a larger model helps only where the design or low-degree units provide support, and otherwise trades bias for leverage.

issues.quote: richer regressions reduce bias only where the graph supplies extreme exposures
issues.why: Table 6's ER, k=4, Bernoulli row gives bias −0.45 for ols-s and +0.01 for the cubic, despite Section 6.2 reporting 0.0% extreme exposures on ER. The cubic reduces bias there but increases RMSE to 1.92; the claim needs to distinguish bias reduction from an improvement in total error.

issues.quote: but it has the lowest RMSE when the response is steep and the linear model badly wrong (threshold, Bernoulli: $0.52$ vs $1.47$ on ER, $0.26$ vs $0.38$ on Stanford3, $0.41$ vs $0.61$ on ego-Facebook)
issues.why: Table 6 reports threshold/Bernoulli cubic RMSE 0.09 versus boosting 0.26 on Stanford3, and 0.18 versus 0.41 on ego-Facebook. Boosting beats the linear fit in these examples but is not the lowest-RMSE regression reported.

issues.quote: Over 63 (graph, shape, degree, $n$) Bernoulli settings the simulated bias differs from it by at most $0.012$ (median $0.003$) on a GATE of $\approx2$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:ext}a).
issues.why: E2.csv has 18 ols_s Bernoulli rows at regular degree 128 with fail=1 and missing bias/RMSE, leaving 60 evaluable settings rather than 63. The zero-degree-spread normalization in sim.py:65 contaminates outcomes, so the stated sweep coverage includes unmeasured settings.

issues.quote: Combining the closed-form bias and leverage, $\sqrt{B^2+\hat\kappa^2L/n}$ matches the observed RMSE with median ratio $1.005$ (IQR $[0.99,1.03]$; $89\%$ within $\pm10\%$) over 360 world-settings (d).
issues.why: fig_extrap.py:61 divides the within-10% count by all 378 rows, including 18 missing ratios, although the sentence describes 360 valid world-settings. The delivered data give 335/360, approximately 93%, for that valid set; the reported 89% uses 335/378.

issues.quote: Across nine (degree, $n$) combinations on ER graphs, the measured crossover (RMSE ratio $=1$, log-interpolated, mean of 6 worlds) is within $0.67$--$1.02\times$ of $\hat\kappa\sqrt{L/n}$ (Table~\ref{tab:cross}).
issues.why: fig_crossover.py:44 uses the older calibration 1.124, whereas Section 6.1 reports the final fitted value 1.09 (headline_numbers.json: 1.086143272028664). Table 5 and the 0.67–1.02 ratio range therefore compare against a different calibration from the one the text identifies; the qualitative crossover trend remains.

issues.quote: The full-neighbourhood H\'ajek estimator is unbiased when defined
issues.why: sim.py:307–313 implements a self-normalized difference of ratios, which is not generally exactly design-unbiased; conditioning on both arms having a qualifying exposure does not establish unbiasedness. Small empirical biases in selected simulations support an approximate statement, not this unconditional assertion.

issues.quote: Monte-Carlo standard errors of each world's RMSE are $\le0.04\times$RMSE with $R=300$ and are smaller than the across-world spread
issues.why: E1.csv, ols_s/Stanford3/cluster/target K=10/world 3, has rmse_se=0.019700247746423375 and rmse=0.10219950159001966, a ratio of 0.193. Thus the universal 4% bound fails even for the main estimator, although the paper's across-world ranges and few-cluster limitations still show substantial uncertainty.

The proof in sec_appendix_proofs.tex:7 supplies an upper bound using the largest eigenvalue of the score covariance, not equality with that bound. The approximate RMSE equality is an empirical calibration beyond the bound; the paper explicitly acknowledges first-order theory without rates.

presentation.why: The printed script-to-output mapping assigns Figure 4 to fig_crossover.py and Figure 5 to fig_design.py, but the paper displays Figure 4 as design factors and Figure 5 as crossover. This sends a reproducing reader to the wrong scripts.

Additional-results tables float into the checklist: Tables 6–7 occupy page 14, followed by the appendix inference/network-noise figures on page 15, interrupting the checklist begun on page 13. The results are readable but their placement makes the appendix harder to follow.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: With one constant $\hat\kappa=1.09$ fitted on the 72 ER/Bernoulli runs
paper_mismatches.why: The crossover predictor uses the literal 1.124, not the final fitted 1.086143272028664 saved by stats_summary.py:10. This changes Table 5 predictions and the reported observed/predicted crossover range.

The ER Bernoulli table filter pools both tag=shape and tag=n_sweep for ols_s and ols_s_quad, mixing n=1000, 4000 and 16000. Cubic and boosting cells use the primary n=4000 settings, so these cells do not represent the same comparison; for ER k=4, primary ols_s RMSE rounds to 0.49 rather than the table's pooled 0.50.

The implemented walk-statistics predictor fixes every tail statistic psi_k to the last computed psi_K rather than evaluating the infinite series exactly. The paper acknowledges approximate first-order theory, but does not identify this numerical tail approximation beside the 'exact' curve.

Cluster assignment redraws all-treated/all-control cluster allocations at lines 176–180, but Hájek weights use unconditional p**k and (1-p)**k. Under this conditioned design the treated exposure probability is (p**k-p**K)/(1-p**K-(1-p)**K); the discrepancy is negligible for the main balanced many-cluster comparisons but can matter in the few-cluster and small-p sweeps.

evaluation_errors.why: Standardizing constant log degrees divides by zero; line 72 then multiplies NaN by zero and contaminates the baseline outcomes. E2.csv contains 18 failed ols_s Bernoulli world-settings at regular degree 128 (three shapes, six worlds), with fail=1 and missing truth/bias/RMSE, silently reducing the claimed sweep.

The displayed valid count excludes NaN ratios, but the within-10% mean counts their comparisons as false. The same result is described as 360 world-settings with 89% agreement; for those valid settings the delivered rows give 335/360=93.06%, rather than 335/378=88.62%. The central agreement trend survives.

The prediction is evaluated with a stale 1.124 calibration while the reported fitted constant is 1.086143272028664. Correcting the input changes the predictions and crossover-ratio range, while preserving the broad spillover threshold finding.

Pooling ER size-sweep results into only some estimator columns changes reported bias/RMSE cells and makes Table 6's ER comparison inconsistent across estimators. Filtering tag=shape for every primary E2 cell restores the intended matched settings; no main qualitative conclusion needs to reverse.

problems.why: graphs.py:9, experiments.py:13 and ac.py:7–9 assume /work/data, /work/results and /work/paper. The launcher downloads relative to its own directory and the delivered code and paper occupy separate roots, so relocating or running the delivered launcher requires path/layout repair.

run_all_experiments.sh:8 skips the Stanford archive download when the .mtx exists, but line 10 unconditionally hashes the .zip under set -e. The manifest omits that .zip while delivering the .mtx, so this delivery hits a missing-file failure at the checksum step; this is a packaging-sensitive launcher bug.

code/run_all.sh does not stop on a failed experiment, and experiments.py:73–76 catches configuration exceptions and continues. A pipeline can therefore proceed with incomplete results unless the CSV failure fields and logs are checked.

process_notes: Counts use the 57 program_runs entries as the unit of run classification, not each setting, world, process or experiment name within a suite. Pilot/theoretical calculations that produce study results count as experiments; smoke/timing checks do not.

All nine listed failure entries have later recovery evidence: 24→26, 28→30, 32→34, 46/47→48, 90→later E5 results, 125/126→later successful PDF builds, and 178→179. Six are explicitly marked recovered in tables.json; the remaining three recoveries are visible in the detailed record.

Rework counts commands that regenerate already-used numerical or plotted results after the first manuscript use: root#toolu_016niEikGrWgSpED7N2dtX8S, root#toolu_011NyNQxziNF4CPDmForsje6, root#toolu_01DzY1G1p7ycVvkNphXwiaob, root#toolu_014M6ZDp5tVMLzyHnRbouAeB, root#toolu_014sAncBEDFsT53LoWVDGY4p, root#toolu_01H4HBsNwQ1mj4QhfphoAqgy, root#toolu_01Tu9EWJP6nKnVNPtHtHN93V, root#toolu_01TfWgNGbtm9U3rucfFj4dCx, root#toolu_01XZLmgWJexqU3opF1kewao3, root#toolu_01VpqTm8kyT6rDmjHhXvfCWB, root#toolu_01MyRXYSnRznzHKA6p2aFdXU, plus the queued E3 rerun root#toolu_01WSyLEKm4ob9ms3Mrs9QtdX whose completed results are checked later. Multiple artifacts regenerated in one command count once; pure PDF compilation and text-only edits do not count.

fields.json states that detached shell processes are not automatically followed after their launching command returns. Later log-tail commands and result reads supply completion evidence; absence of an automatic job record is not counted as missing experimental work.

integrity.why: The record compares diagnostics and reports their failures as well as successes; it does not show a winning configuration selected by a held-out evaluation score and then presented as an independently tested method. Weighted/stratified fits were added after exploratory heterogeneity results, and the paper explicitly labels their evaluation in-sample; the global prediction scale's ER fitting subset is also disclosed.

Empty-arm redrawing, the smaller boosting experiment, the final six-world protocol and post-exploration diagnostics are documented in the paper/README. The inspected edits do not establish an undisclosed evaluation change made to favor a reported result; the denominator, mixed-setting table and stale-calibration errors are listed separately as code/reporting defects.

These are design-based simulations with known potential outcomes, not a forbidden held-out prediction-label task. Observed outcomes legitimately fit the regressions; all-treated/all-control truth is used for evaluation and theoretical checks. The inspected method/evaluation code and recorded edits show no prohibited evaluation-label input to the fitted estimators.

The main reported numerical sources have experiment launches, observed output, and analysis/table-generating executions. Derived theoretical quantities are computed in those scripts; an older fitted calibration reused as a literal is not evidence of a fabricated result. fields.json limits observation of detached processes, so completion is inferred only where later logs or produced results are actually inspected.
